title: 31 Quasars That Are Too Old to Make Sense
hook: Astronomers found 31 quasars shining from when the universe was just 5% of its current age — powered by black holes that shouldn't have had time to grow so big yet.
key_points: The Euclid space telescope's Wide Survey turned up 31 quasars, including the two earliest ever detected.
These quasars date to when the universe was only about 670 million years old.
They're powered by supermassive black holes ranging from hundreds of millions to billions of times the Sun's mass.
Existing theories of black hole growth can't yet explain how they got that massive that early.
content_html: Quasars are among the brightest objects in the universe, powered by supermassive black holes devouring surrounding matter. Finding them from the universe's earliest days is a direct test of how fast such enormous black holes can actually form — and a new haul of them is straining that theory.
extra_html: Using data from the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope, launched in 2023, a team led by lead author Daming Yang with Joseph Hennawi (UC Santa Barbara and Leiden University) identified 31 ancient quasars, including the two earliest ever detected. These objects date from when the universe was only about 670 million years old — roughly 5% of its current age — and are powered by black holes ranging from hundreds of millions to billions of times the mass of the Sun. That's the puzzle: standard models of black hole growth don't have an obvious way to pack in that much mass so quickly. "These monsters...somehow already existed when the universe was in its infancy," Hennawi said. "We don't yet have a good understanding of how they grew so massive, so fast." Published in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

related.title: The Big Bang
related.hook: About 13.8 billion years ago the universe began hot and dense and has been expanding ever since — but it wasn't an explosion into empty space. Space itself stretched.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

related.title: Why Does Webb Keep Finding Things That Shouldn't Exist?
related.hook: JWST keeps spotting early black holes and galaxies that are too big, too bright, or too early to fit standard models — and cosmologists are racing to figure out which of many new theories is right.

flashcards.prompt: What did the Euclid space telescope's Wide Survey find?
flashcards.back_html: 31 ancient quasars, including the two earliest ever detected, dating from when the universe was only about 670 million years old.

flashcards.prompt: Why do these quasars challenge existing theories of black hole growth?

choices.text: Their supermassive black holes reached hundreds of millions to billions of solar masses far too soon after the Big Bang
They appear to be moving away from Earth faster than light
They contain no detectable matter at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Standard models of black hole growth struggle to explain how black holes could accumulate that much mass in the roughly 670 million years available since the Big Bang.

flashcards.prompt: What does a quasar actually get its brightness from?
flashcards.back_html: A supermassive black hole at a galaxy's center, pulling in surrounding matter that heats up and glows intensely as it falls in.
